name: Lena Evans

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Lena, thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I teach English at Riverside Community School, a mixed comprehensive on the edge of the city, mostly Years 9 to 11 plus one A-level group. My day is four or five lessons, a detention duty, and a lot of essays: I use an AI assistant every morning to draft feedback on them, then I rewrite it in my own words. The best bit is when a quiet fifteen-year-old reads out a poem they wrote and the room goes silent. The worst bit is the behaviour emails, dozens a day.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And at home? Who's there, and how's money?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my partner Jonah, who's a freelance illustrator, in a rented flat with a damp bathroom. His commissions have dropped by about a third this year because clients are making pictures with AI instead. So I'm carrying more of the rent than I used to, and we've got about two and a half months saved. I also run the school's little AI working group, which is funny given how left-wing I am about the tech companies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a decent tool that got oversold by people with something to sell. I'd post a slightly told-you-so thread about the tech bosses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For my job, nothing much: I keep using the feedback drafts and saving a few hours a week. The bit that doesn't go away is Jonah. The clients who left for cheap AI pictures aren't coming back just because the hype died down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep teaching and keep using the tools the way I do now. I'd pick up the paid training sessions I've been asked to run for other schools in the trust, about two hundred a session, because we need it. And we'd keep a tight grip on the food shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine about me, a bit heavy about us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Jonah's work has already taken a hit. Does a plateau undo any of that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, not really. The cheap end of illustration has gone for good, I think. He's moving towards teaching art workshops, which is a strange thing to watch: the AI pushes him into my world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You run the AI working group. What happens to that in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It probably shrinks into a once-a-term thing. I'd be a bit sad, honestly; I like being the person who understands it. I'd still run the training for other schools while they want it.

say: I'd say AI is a **decent tool** that was oversold by people with something to sell.
I'd post a told-you-so thread about the **tech bosses**.
think: I think my own job stays **the same**, with a few hours saved each week.
Jonah's lost **illustration clients** won't come back just because the hype died down.
do: Keep drafting essay feedback with **AI** and rewriting it myself.
Run **paid training** for other trust schools at about £200 a session.
Keep a tight grip on the **food shop**.
feel: **Fine** about her own work, **heavy** about the household's money.
S0.quote: The clients who left for cheap AI pictures aren't coming back just because the hype died down.
fieldNote: Already living with AI's impact through her **partner's illustration work**.
An **enthusiastic user** who still distrusts the companies selling the tools.
Paid trust training is a real **side income** she'd pursue even in the quiet world.

steps.text: Keep using the AI assistant to draft essay feedback
Run paid AI training sessions for other trust schools
Keep teaching Years 9 to 11 and the A-level group

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say schools need a proper public plan, not every head buying whichever app had the slickest salesperson. I'd want the union to set the rules on this, and I'd help write them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'm well placed. I already know the tools better than most of the department, so I'd be the one showing people how. The real problem is Jonah: any more of his work goes, and we're on one salary in a city.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd volunteer to lead AI in English for the whole trust, which might come with a pay point. I'd take more paid training work in the holidays. I'd push the union for a policy before the trust writes one. And we'd move every spare pound into savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited and worried in the same breath, which is exhausting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to English teaching specifically when AI takes over writing and checking?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marking essays becomes a smaller part of English teaching, which I won't miss. Getting a kid to say what they actually think grows. So does reading together and arguing about a poem. The fear is a manager deciding one teacher can do that with forty kids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If Jonah's income dropped further, what would you cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car first, then the takeaways. Then we'd look at a cheaper flat, which hurts because the commute would be awful.

say: I'd say schools need a **public plan**, not heads buying the slickest app.
I'd want the **union** to set the rules, and I'd help write them.
think: I think I'm **well placed**, because I already know the tools better than most.
The real risk is **one salary** in a city if Jonah loses more work.
do: Volunteer to lead **AI in English** across the trust, hopefully with a pay point.
Take more **paid training** work during school holidays.
feel: **Excited** and **worried** at once, which she finds exhausting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs an emergency response like a pandemic: income support, a pause on school staffing cuts, and public ownership of the big models. I'd be very loud about it online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worse, honestly. I know how good it already is at feedback. If it's better than me at explaining poems by 2028, my job becomes keeping order while kids use it. Jonah's illustration work would be finished, so we'd both be scrambling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'd start applying to the trust's central AI team, because being the person who sets the system up buys time. We'd cut to basics and probably move in with my sister in the next town to save rent. And I'd join whichever campaign was pushing for income support.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Panicky in my chest, even though my head's making lists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use these tools every day. Does that make this picture better or worse for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Knowing how good AI already is at feedback makes AGI by 2028 worse for me, not better. I'm not in denial about it, which means I can see exactly where this goes. People who don't use it still think it can't write a decent paragraph.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With robots coming three years after AGI, what's left in a school between 2028 and 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Supervision, safeguarding, behaviour, the stuff that needs a body in the room. That's real, but it's not what I trained for, and it would pay less. I'd do it, though. You'd have to.

say: I'd call for an **emergency response**: income support and a pause on staffing cuts.
I'd argue loudly for **public ownership** of the big AI models.
think: I think my job turns into **keeping order** while kids learn from the AI.
Jonah's **illustration work** would be finished, so we'd both be scrambling.
do: Apply to the trust's **central AI team** this month to buy time.
Move in with **my sister** in the next town to save rent.
Join the campaign for **income support** for displaced workers.
feel: **Panic** in her chest while her head keeps making lists.
S2.quote: Knowing how good AI already is at feedback makes AGI by 2028 worse for me, not better.
fieldNote: Her daily use makes her **more alarmed**, not less; she knows the tools' strength.
Expects her role to shrink to **supervision and safeguarding** in the robot gap.
Would **move in with family** to protect the cushion, a quick practical step.

steps.text: Apply for a job on the trust's central AI team

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to set rules if we start now. I'd push the union to treat this like the biggest bargaining issue in a generation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it means I have a short window where knowing the tools is valuable, and then it isn't. The smart move is to build something human on top: pastoral work, mentoring, counselling. Jonah has maybe two good years left freelancing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a part-time counselling diploma next year, evenings, about two thousand pounds over two years. I'd keep leading AI work at school while it counts. We'd try to get to five months of savings, and Jonah would take a teaching assistant job for steady money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but busy, and busy helps me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you do differently with five years instead of two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Head of year or a school counsellor. The kids will still be fifteen and miserable about something, and a person sitting with them still matters. I'd like to be that person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would you want to be by 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a race between the tools and my diploma. Five years feels just about long enough to win.

I'd push the union to treat AI as the biggest **bargaining issue** in a generation.
think: I think knowing the tools is **valuable briefly**, then it isn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is plenty of time to do this fairly, so no excuses. If governments waste it, voters should remember.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think ten years suits me: I'm adaptable, I'll have the counselling qualification, and I'll know the AI tools inside out. It's the people who haven't touched AI that I'd worry about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still do the counselling diploma, just over three years. I'd put a bit into a pension top-up and maybe an index fund, because I'll want options at forty. And I'd campaign locally for an AI plan for schools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hopeful, honestly, with a little background hum.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, does the household picture change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. Jonah would have time to build a proper second career, maybe teaching art. We could think about a baby around thirty-two without feeling reckless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be thirty-seven in 2036. What does that version of you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Runs pastoral care for a school, probably, and still marks the odd poem for fun. Maybe trains other teachers on the people side, which the machines won't do.

say: I'd say a **decade** is plenty of time, so there are no excuses.
If governments **waste it**, voters should remember.
think: I think ten years **suits me**, because I'm adaptable and will be qualified.
I'd worry more about colleagues who've **never touched AI**.
do: Take the **counselling diploma** more slowly, over three years.
Start a **pension top-up** and a small index fund.
Campaign locally for a **school AI plan**.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because both Jonah and I are in exposed work and there'd be no time. What would help is real income support while people retrain, and funded counselling and pastoral posts in schools so teachers can move into them.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about partners. Lots of teachers live with people in exposed jobs, and the household matters more than the job title. My teaching job looks fine on paper while my partner's illustration work goes.
